The Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (commonly known as the Alliance) was accused in a subversion case. Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, who pleaded not guilty, underwent a 24-day trial and faced the verdict on August 21. "集誌社" (FactWire News Agency) reviewed the memorable scenes and exchanges in court, allowing readers to revisit the key points of their testimony. It was 1997, the June Fourth anniversary, in Victoria Park. Lee Cheuk-yan, wearing a black T-shirt printed with "Don't want to remember! Dare not forget!", held a microphone and read out in English: "Some say this is the last candlelight vigil we will hold to support the democratic movement, and the last night for China's democracy. Dear compatriots, this is absolutely not true. After the handover, the Alliance will continue to hold the candlelight vigil in Victoria Park every year..." At the time, 40-year-old Lee Cheuk-yan had dark hair and rounded cheeks. Nearly 30 years later, now 68 and with a head of white hair, Lee Cheuk-yan sat in the dock, watched himself on the screen, clenched his fist in front of his nose, pressed his lips lightly, and wiped away tears with his fingers. This veteran of the Alliance, charged with inciting subversion of state power, pleaded not guilty and took the stand to testify about his June Fourth experiences and the Alliance's beliefs. He wept while watching old footage of June Fourth vigils, choked up recalling the plight of the underprivileged, and did not shy away from admitting that after the National Security Law he still adhered to the five core demands, all because it was "based on love for the people." Related reports on the Alliance case: Alliance case – Trial notes | Chow Hang-tung's "intent"; Alliance case | 24-day trial, verdict on 8.21 – Summary of nine key factual and legal issues

Lee Cheuk-yan was imprisoned in April 2021 due to the August 18 unrecognised assembly case. By the time of the verdict, he had been deprived of liberty for over 5 years and 4 months.

Born into a comfortable life, raised in a China of suffering, determined to shoulder the responsibility

On the 13th day of the trial, Lee Cheuk-yan, with a head of white hair, wearing a dark grey long-sleeved shirt and a black down vest, stepped onto the witness stand. He smiled and nodded to the public gallery, swore on the Catholic Bible, and began his testimony.

Lee Cheuk-yan's more than 40-year career in the labour movement and politics began during his university years. Entering the Department of Civil Engineering at the University of Hong Kong in 1975, he encountered the "recognise China, concern society" (認中關社)思潮 there, learned about Wei Jingsheng's proposal of the "Fifth Modernisation" — democracy — and, coming from a well-off family, participated in hall associations and grassroots movements, which had a profound impact on him.

He recalled visiting boat-dwellers (艇戶), and when a child drowned, he could not help but choke up, as if the scene from over 40 years ago was replaying in his mind. He said that his generation was a product of the times — born into a suffering China, they had a responsibility to bear. After graduating, he decided not to practise civil engineering, but to "do something" for Hong Kong society and for China.

"Under that background, I began my life's...," he smiled. "I never expected that I would end up doing it for a lifetime." His leading counsel, Andrew Shum, asked: "A lifetime of what?" Lee Cheuk-yan replied: "A lifetime of labour movement, and of caring about China's democracy."

Lee Cheuk-yan recalled in court how he was influenced by the "recognise China, concern society"思潮 during his university years, and since then devoted himself to grassroots concerns, trade unions and the democracy movement. (Facebook photo)

Baptised by June Fourth, supporting the democracy movement became a lifelong commitment

Afterwards, Lee Cheuk-yan devoted himself to the labour movement while continuing to care about China's pro-democracy movement. When the 1989 pro-democracy movement broke out, the 32-year-old was working as an executive officer at the Christian Industrial Committee. He recalled that after Hu Yaobang's death in April 1989, Beijing students gathered in Tiananmen Square to express their demands against corruption and official profiteering. Hongkongers marched to the Xinhua News Agency and staged sit-ins in solidarity; he was among them, serving as march marshal.

After Beijing students went on hunger strike, over a million Hongkongers marched in solidarity on two occasions, and on May 27 held the "Democratic Songs Dedicated to China" concert at the Happy Valley racecourse, raising approximately HK$12 million. On May 21, Szeto Wah announced the formation of the Alliance; a little over a week later, Lee Cheuk-yan and other Alliance representatives headed to Beijing with HK$1 million in donations.

Lee Cheuk-yan was detained after June Fourth. He described how Hong Kong citizens demanded his release and "saved" him, giving him even greater determination to continue supporting China's pro-democracy movement. (Facebook photo)

In Tiananmen Square, he witnessed students, workers and intellectuals demanding the retraction of the April 26 editorial that characterised the movement as a "turmoil." "They really wanted to tell the authorities... I am a patriot, I just hope the country does well, this patriotic sentiment was extremely strong at the time." On the night of June 3, while he was in the workers' tent, he was suddenly asked to leave. "They said the army had charged in, and they were going out to block the troops." He returned to the hotel and stayed awake all night. "Watching outside, hearing the gunfire, watching Tiananmen Square..." He fell silent for a while. "Around four o'clock... the lights went out."

After June Fourth, Lee Cheuk-yan evacuated with supporters, students and journalists, but on the chartered flight back to Hong Kong, he was asked by public security officers to disembark. He was detained for two days, had the donations confiscated, signed a statement of repentance, and was then allowed to return to Hong Kong.

Having witnessed the dead and wounded being transported in pedicarts along Chang'an Avenue in Tiananmen Square, and later hearing testimonies of the massacre, he described June Fourth as another baptism. "At the time, Beijing citizens told us to tell the whole world what we had seen"; and during his detention, Hong Kong citizens marched to the Governor's House and the Xinhua News Agency to demand his release — "It was Hong Kong citizens who saved me." After returning to Hong Kong, he decided to continue supporting China's pro-democracy movement, to bring democracy to China and Hong Kong. "I felt I had even more responsibility — it became a lifelong commitment."

After being detained, Lee Cheuk-yan had the donations confiscated and signed a statement of repentance before being allowed to return to Hong Kong. Signing the statement of repentance became a lifelong regret. (Facebook photo)

Adhering to the five core demands: autocracy and democracy are incompatible

The Alliance, whose full name is "Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China," was officially established in early June 1989; Lee Cheuk-yan was one of the first standing committee members. He explained that the organisation was positioned to support movements initiated within China, welcoming all those who shared the same ideals, including pro-China groups, and had always been peaceful and non-violent. Until 2020, every June Fourth vigil had received a letter of no objection from the police.

As for the "five core demands" that the Alliance has always upheld, Lee Cheuk-yan said the demands had never changed and were "interlinked": first, demanding the release of imprisoned individuals; then, acknowledging that the movement was a patriotic democratic movement, and that the massacre and suppression were wrong; followed by holding those responsible accountable; and carrying on the demands of the 1989 movement — demanding an end to one-party dictatorship, so that the people could enjoy freedoms of speech, association and the press, and a civil society could be built, providing a foundation to discuss democracy and the system best suited to China. He explained that an autocracy, which concentrates executive, legislative and judicial powers to suppress and punish the people's voices, is incompatible with democracy — without ending autocracy, building a democratic China is "fundamentally impossible."

Lee Cheuk-yan emphasised that the Alliance played a supporting role, and had not discussed what system China should adopt, nor had it reached that stage: "If China has no freedom, if the people have no freedom, there is nothing to discuss." He also disagreed that "ending one-party dictatorship" equals "ending Communist Party leadership": "Whether the Communist Party leads or not is not for us to say — it is for the people to say."

The Alliance was established in early June 1989; Lee Cheuk-yan (first from right) was also a member of its first standing committee. (File photo)

Facing challenges with a relaxed expression and a hint of a smile

During his testimony, Lee Cheuk-yan appeared relaxed and spoke calmly, as if addressing the media countless times before. He answered each question with ease, crisply and directly, and at times with a touch of humour.

When the prosecution asked whether he did not wish the Communist Party to continue ruling, he spread his hands and laughed: "Disagree — that's up to the people to decide, we are not in a position to agree or disagree." When the prosecution suggested he believed intra-party reform within the CCP would not achieve an end to one-party dictatorship, he disagreed, chuckling: "Don't box the Communist Party in like that," drawing laughter from the public gallery.

When the judge asked whether he had paid attention to the 2018 constitutional amendment, he laughed and said: "To be frank, I didn't pay much attention, because I thought Communist Party leadership is a given at any time — I don't need to do anything about it." He also said: "I noticed they had inserted 'Communist Party leadership' into it, and my reaction at the time was — was that even necessary? Everyone knows that anyway." As for whether he wanted more people to put "ending one-party dictatorship" into practice, he laughed and said he thought the question was a false one: "If we were asking people to take action, we wouldn't say 'go do things to end one-party dictatorship' — we wouldn't put it that way."

The prosecution alleged that the 2018 constitutional amendment meant one of the Alliance's five core demands — "end one-party dictatorship" — equated to ending Communist Party leadership, violated the national constitution and constituted unlawful means.

"I have no hostility in my heart, only love"

The prosecution questioned Lee Cheuk-yan twice about whether he harboured hostility towards the CCP. The first time, Deputy Senior Public Prosecutor Vicki Lai asked whether he held "extreme hostility" towards CCP rule of the country; Lee Cheuk-yan shook his head: "Disagree." Lai rephrased and asked if he held "at least some hostility"; Lee immediately replied: "I have no hostility in my heart, only love. It is based on love for the people; I hope the Communist Party will reform, so that the people can enjoy the rights and happiness they deserve."

On another occasion, Lai pointed out that Lee Cheuk-yan had consistently advocated "ending one-party dictatorship" and wanted more people to harbour hostility towards the CCP. He denied this again, stressing more firmly that he wanted the public to make demands of the CCP, hoping it would respect democracy and human rights — "It shouldn't be called hostility."

Lai asked Lee Cheuk-yan a series of questions about his views on the CCP. "Do you agree that the Alliance and you have always regarded the Chinese Communist Party as an authoritarian regime?" Lee tilted his head, thought for a few seconds, then answered: "Before '49 it was not an authoritarian regime; after the founding of the state, it was." He also agreed, one by one, with the prosecution's other characterisations: that the Alliance believed the CCP "strangled the voices of the people, especially dissenting voices," "strangled democracy," "suppressed the people through the state system," "violated human rights," held "no elections with genuine popular participation," and regarded the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) as "a token."

"Then do you agree that the Alliance considers that the Chinese Communist Party's rule of the country is, in practice, one-party dictatorship?" "I agree, but it should not be one-party dictatorship," Lee said.

Lee Cheuk-yan denied harbouring hostility towards the CCP, saying: "I have no hostility in my heart, only love."

"I am of course absolutely patriotic"

After Lee Cheuk-yan denied hostility towards CCP leadership, the prosecution reframed the question, suggesting he was "dissatisfied" with CCP leadership and believed it was "bad for the country." Lee said he "praised what was right and condemned what was wrong," welcoming some policies while being dissatisfied with others, and that what dissatisfied him most was "the people having no voice, no basic rights." He also openly acknowledged that he had learned to organise trade unions from the Communist Party: "When I was young, I really admired the Communist Party."

Under persistent questioning from the prosecution, he added: "It is bad for the country, but we hope it will be even better for the country and the people," and reiterated: "I emphasise, I hope it does well." Judge Andrew Chan asked: "Meaning the Communist Party?" Lee answered: "Yes, I hope the Communist Party does well."

Loving the country does not mean loving the Party — that is perhaps one way to understand the Alliance's beliefs. In its opening statement, the prosecution noted that during a protest in 2012, Lee Cheuk-yan had said: "We are absolutely patriotic, but we believe that if we are to love the country, we must end one-party dictatorship — that is what it truly means to be patriotic."

Lee Cheuk-yan's counsel, in his final question in the examination-in-chief, asked him — since the Alliance's full name included "patriotic," did he love the country?

"I think once I entered university, I already felt that a suffering China must have a tomorrow. From that point on I hoped the country would develop and become prosperous, democratic and free. I had already resolved at that time to hope that China would have a good future for its people. I am of course absolutely patriotic," Lee Cheuk-yan said.

When asked whether he loved the country, Lee Cheuk-yan said he was "absolutely patriotic," and that since entering university he had hoped the country would develop and become prosperous, democratic and free. (File photo)
